issues.legal_issue: A registered instrument takes effect from its execution date when the applicable law would have allowed it to operate from that date without registration.
material_facts: The lease was executed before the date on which the land was said to vest in the State, but it was registered after that date.
The plaintiff relied on the lease to establish title to the land.
issues.conclusion: The registered lease operated from its execution date, so the land did not vest in the State before the plaintiff acquired title.
issues.legal_principle: Section 47 of the Registration Act provides that a registered document operates from the time it would have commenced to operate if registration had not been required. Although an unregistered document is not valid while it remains unregistered, once registered it takes effect from its execution date. The Court relied on Ram Saran Lall v. Mst Domini Kuer and Nanda Ballabh Gururani v. Smt Maqbool Begum; it therefore rejected the argument based on Section 6 of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights Act.

predicates.title_dispute_over_registered_instrument: The proceeding concerns a claim to title based on a registered instrument.
predicates.instrument_executed_before_claimed_vesti: The instrument was executed before the date on which the opposing party claims the property vested elsewhere.
predicates.instrument_registered_after_claimed_vest: The instrument was registered after the claimed vesting date.

issues.definition: When a title dispute involves an instrument executed before a claimed vesting date but registered afterward, the instrument operates from its execution.

issues.legal_issue: The requirements applicable to leases under the general property-transfer law cannot be applied to an agricultural lease when that law excludes agricultural leases and the governing tenancy law does not impose an equivalent requirement.
material_facts: The disputed lease concerned agricultural land.
The lease was executed by the landholder's representative and was not signed by the lessee.
The governing state tenancy law provided for execution of leases but contained no provision equivalent to the general property-transfer law's requirement invoked against the lease.
issues.conclusion: The lease was not invalid merely because the lessee had not signed it under the requirements of the general property-transfer law.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 117 and 107 of the Transfer of Property Act were considered. Section 117 excludes agricultural leases from the Act, so Section 107 does not govern them. The principles contained in Section 107 cannot be extended to agricultural leases where the state tenancy law provides for execution of leases without an equivalent requirement.

predicates.agricultural_lease_dispute: The proceeding concerns a lease of agricultural land.
predicates.lease_signed_only_by_landholder: The lease was executed by the landholder or the landholder's representative, but not signed by the lessee.
predicates.agricultural_leases_excluded_from_genera: The general law invoked to require a particular form of execution excludes agricultural leases from its operation.
predicates.governing_tenancy_law_lacks_equivalent_e: The applicable tenancy law provides for execution of leases but does not impose the equivalent formality relied on to invalidate the lease.

issues.definition: An agricultural lease executed by the landholder is not invalid for lack of the lessee's signature when the general transfer law does not govern it and the applicable tenancy law imposes no equivalent formality.

issues.legal_issue: Permissive possession becomes adverse only when cogent and convincing evidence establishes hostile possession to the knowledge of the true owner.
material_facts: The person claiming adverse possession initially entered the land under a licence to operate a brick-kiln.
The appellate court considered the evidence and found that the possession was not adverse.
No cogent evidence established hostile animus and possession adverse to the knowledge of the true owner.
issues.conclusion: The person in possession did not acquire rights by adverse possession; the permissive possession did not become adverse merely through its duration.
issues.legal_principle: A licensee's, agent's, co-owner's, or other permissive possession must be shown by cogent and convincing evidence to involve hostile animus and possession adverse to the knowledge of the real owner. Mere possession for any length of time does not convert permissive possession into adverse possession.

predicates.adverse_possession_claim_in_possession_s: A person resisting a claim for possession asserts that they acquired rights by adverse possession.
predicates.possession_began_with_permission: The person asserting adverse possession initially entered or remained in possession with the owner's permission.
predicates.cogent_evidence_of_hostility_known_to_ow: Cogent and convincing evidence shows hostile possession adverse to the true owner and brought to that owner's knowledge.

issues.definition: A person who began in permissive possession does not acquire title by adverse possession unless cogent evidence shows hostile possession known to the true owner.

issues.legal_issue: A factual finding on adverse possession supported by the evidence cannot be reopened through an attempt to reweigh that evidence in the further appellate proceedings described in this case.
material_facts: The trial court found adverse possession, but the appellate court reversed that finding after considering the evidence and decreed possession for the plaintiff.
The High Court did not interfere with the appellate court's factual finding in second appeal.
In the further appeal, the appellant sought to rely again on the parties' evidence and a commissioner's map, but the Court found no injustice requiring intervention.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to reappraise the evidence or disturb the appellate court's finding that possession was not adverse.
issues.legal_principle: The Court stated that re-examination of the evidence was not permissible even in second appeal, much less in the exercise of jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution, and noted that no injustice requiring remedy had been shown.

rule.if: further_appeal_under_special_leave and lower_court_factual_finding_on_adverse_possession and appellant_seeks_evidentiary_reassessment and no_injustice_shown

predicates.further_appeal_under_special_leave: The matter reaches the Supreme Court in a further appeal invoking its special-leave jurisdiction after a second appeal.
predicates.lower_court_factual_finding_on_adverse_p: The appellate court has made a factual finding about whether possession was adverse, and that finding was left undisturbed in second appeal.
predicates.appellant_seeks_evidentiary_reassessment: The appellant asks the further appellate court to reconsider the evidence underlying the finding.
predicates.no_injustice_shown: The appellant has not shown an injustice requiring intervention.

issues.definition: When a further appeal asks for reassessment of an undisturbed factual finding on adverse possession and no injustice is shown, the finding is not reopened.
